passage:
On the first Monday of December, Ottilie Renk sorted the Havering post twice. The second sorting took four minutes and produced one envelope, addressed in a hand she had known since she was nineteen, which she carried into the back room and laid in the drawer under the scales. In January she took it out again and put it in a tin that had once held boiled sweets, on the shelf above the stove, where by then there were thirty of its fellows. She had never opened one. She had never told anybody the tin was there.

The village had its theories, because the village always did. Mrs. Prell at the shop held that Ottilie had been sweet on Bryn Cadoc since before the war and could not bear to see his letters go to a woman in Tarne. The schoolmaster, who was fond of a grievance, held that the Havering office had been slovenly for years and that a letter went astray there most winters. Ottilie's own sister held that it was kindness: that Ilse Mawer had been ill a long time and did not need a letter every December from a man who had gone away in 1961 and not come back.

None of the three had been in the sorting room on the morning Bryn Cadoc came in with his coat still wet and set the first of them on the counter. He did not ask her to post it. He asked her to hold it, and to go on holding it, until he came in a second time and asked for it by name — until he asked twice, was how he put it, and she remembered thinking it a strange, lawyerly way of speaking for a man she had never heard use a word of more than two syllables. She said she would. He put his hat back on and went out into Marsh Street, and he had not asked again.

Thirty-one Decembers is a long while to keep a small promise that nobody has been told about. Ottilie had had leisure to consider that the promise had been a foolish one to make; that Bryn had very likely forgotten it inside a month; that Ilse Mawer might have been glad of the letters, or might not, and that there was no way now of finding out which. She had considered all of it, standing at the scales with the envelope in her hand, and had gone on putting them in the tin. What she had undertaken was not to decide whether the letters should arrive. It was to wait until she was asked a second time. She did not say that this was wise. She said that it was what she had said.

a habit Ottilie had fallen into and could no longer account for
a fondness for the sender that Ottilie had never admitted to anybody
a disorder in the office that Ottilie had let go on too long
a wish to spare the woman the letters were addressed to

prompt: The passage is chiefly concerned with a collection of casts that
passage:
Between 1908 and 1931 the Farne Institute bought two hundred and six plaster casts of classical heads for its teaching collection, and entered every one of them in the register as the work of the Bramm workshop in Leipzig. Bramm's name was a guarantee. The firm took its moulds from the marbles themselves, under licence, in Rome and Naples and Munich, and its casts were bought by schools that could not send their pupils to see the originals.

In 1994 Imre Vass set out to check the register, and the instrument he used was shrinkage. Plaster taken from a mould comes out very slightly smaller than the thing the mould was taken from; a cast made from a mould taken off another cast is smaller again, by about the same fraction a second time. The difference is under a millimetre across a human head, but it is consistent, and Vass had the published measurements of the marbles to compare against. He measured the same three dimensions on every one of the two hundred and six.

The figures fell into two groups. A hundred and forty-five sat where a first cast should sit. Sixty-one sat a further step down, and they answer to one another closely but not to the rest. Vass then did the thing the register made easy: he looked up when each of the sixty-one had come in. Every one of them had been bought between 1919 and 1923, and no cast bought in those five years fell into the other group.

Bramm's own papers explain what the Institute could not have known. The firm's moulding shop was under water in the winter of 1918 and out of use for four years, and its printed catalogue for 1920 is the largest it ever issued. A workshop that is selling more heads than it can mould must be getting them from somewhere, and the somewhere leaves its mark in the plaster.

The Institute was told once. The minutes of the Standing Committee for March 1923 record a curator's complaint that the new heads “do not take the light as the older ones do, being softer in the feature”. The complaint was minuted, thanked, and not acted upon, and it is the only contemporary notice of a difference that anyone could have measured with a pair of callipers at any time in the seventy years that followed. Vass says so twice.
choices: includes a group mixed with a plaster the firm never used
was made in the Institute's own workshop and sold under a maker's name
includes a group taken from moulds made off other casts
had been repaired far more often than the register admitted
was bought from two firms whose invoices had been confused

prompt: The passage is chiefly concerned with a record that
passage:
Sylvia Reece was warden of Bewl Heath for twenty-two years, and for each of those years she wrote down the date on which she first saw an adder out of the ground. The heath is small — five banks of dry sand and heather, none of them ten minutes' walk from the next — and she walked all five on the same route, from the car park at Tolt End to the stile above the pit and back. Her first date was the eleventh of March. Her last was the twentieth of February. Over the run of the record the first sighting came forward by nineteen days.

She is careful about what this is. A record of this kind, she writes in the note that accompanies it, is only as sound as the walking behind it, and a date is not a measurement of the adders but of the meeting between the adders and the warden.

In 2004 she began walking the heath weekly instead of fortnightly. She had retired that spring and had the time for it. The route did not change and the banks did not change, but from 2004 the record has twice as many chances each February to catch a snake on its first morning out, and eleven of the nineteen days were gained after that year.

The clearance is a cleaner question. Scrub was taken off the two banks above the pit in 1998 and the other three were left alone. If the opening of those banks to the sun were what was moving the dates, the two cleared banks should have run ahead of the other three from 1999 onward. They did not. Cleared and uncleared come forward together, within a day or two of each other, in every year of the record after 1998.

February temperatures at the nearest station rose over the same twenty-two years; that much is not in dispute, and Reece does not dispute it. What she disputes is the use that has been made of her figure. Nineteen days has now appeared twice in print as evidence of a warming climate, in one case without her name on it and in the other with it, and she has written to both. Her record cannot be evidence of that, she says, because she cannot take her own boots out of it.
choices: advanced sharply and then returned to where it had begun
was given up when the warden's route had to be changed
agrees closely with records kept on three other heaths
advanced over twenty-two years and cannot be put down to one cause
was kept from memory rather than from notes and proved more exact than expected

prompt: The writer argues chiefly that worn lettering on a village war memorial should be
passage:
A memorial that has been re-cut is a memorial that has been replaced, and I would rather have the worn one. This is not a fashionable position and I want to put it as flatly as I can: when the lettering on a village war memorial goes shallow, the parish should leave it shallow.

Chaldon re-cut its memorial in 2011. The lettering had gone soft — the stone is a limestone that takes a beautiful letter and does not keep it — and the parish raised eleven hundred pounds and had the whole roll of honour cut again, in the same face, in the same places, a good deal deeper than the original. The mason did excellent work. The result is a memorial that looks as though the men on it died recently. Ninety years of weather came off that stone in three days, and nothing on it now is older than the youngest thing in the village.

I will allow one exception and it is narrower than it sounds. Where a name has become unreadable — not shallow, not faint in a raking light, but gone, so that a family standing in front of the stone cannot find the man they came for — the stone has stopped doing the one thing it was put up to do, and the name should be cut again. That is not a licence to re-cut the memorial. It is a licence to re-cut a name; and at Chaldon every name could still be read, as the photographs taken before the work prove.

I do not think the parishes that do this are careless of their memorials. They are the opposite. They are tidy people, and a war memorial standing in the middle of a mown green with everything about it kept and painted and weeded is an offence to tidiness the moment the letters blur. Nobody has ever asked them to examine the wish; the mason is glad of the order; and money is easy to raise for a purpose nobody can be seen to object to.

But the memorial's office is not to be legible. The parish council is the corporation that owns the stone. It is not the corporation that owns the ninety years. The wear is the one part of a memorial that cannot be commissioned, and Chaldon paid eleven hundred pounds to have its only irreplaceable feature taken off.

prompt: The passage is chiefly concerned with a chamber whose purpose
passage:
Under the north-west corner of the farmhouse at Dunmarry there is a stone chamber eleven feet by seven, barrel-vaulted, with a flagged floor and a single window the size of a folded newspaper high in the outer wall. Everybody in the townland knows what it is. It is where the Herrons hid in 1798, and the story has been told in that form for as long as anyone has been asking, and it went into the Antiquarian's county volume in 1888 without a question mark.

The door is against it. The chamber is entered from the dairy passage by a doorway with its original jambs, and the jambs carry the sockets for a bar — on the passage side. A room barred from outside is a room for keeping things in. A family shutting themselves in would have wanted the bar on their own side of the door, and there was never one there. The window settles what is left of the story: it is unglazed, it has never had a shutter, and it looks out over the yard at the height of a standing man.

The floor is worth as much as the door. It is flagged; the flags are laid to a fall of about an inch in seven feet; and at the low corner there is a drain that runs out under the wall and is open still.

Here the case stops, and I want to be honest about where. A flagged floor sloped to a drain is what you would build for a dairy, and it is also what you would build for a retting and drying room for flax, which was the other trade of that townland until the 1840s. The chamber is cool and it is dark, and both trades wanted cool and dark. No churn, no vessel, no scutching blade and no fragment of either trade came out of the floor when it was lifted in 1974, and the farm accounts that survive begin in 1851, after the flax had gone. I have been in the chamber a dozen times and I could not tell you which it was, and I know of nothing short of a new excavation that would.

What I will say is that the vault is bonded into the outer wall, course for course, and went up when the house went up. Whatever it was for, it was wanted from the first.
